What is in the course?
GCSE Separate Science (Triple Science) is offered to most students from the beginning of year 9. How is it assessed?

Over the course of their science GCSE, the student’s attainment is reviewed to see if the examination they sit should be the separate sciences or the combined science. This is to allow for some students who we believe would benefit from the attainment level for each GCSE grade on combined science being lower than for triple award and it is hoped they will attain higher on the combined GCSE than on the triple award GCSE’s.
Students will take formal written examinations at the end of Year 11. There are no module examinations and the course follows a linear structure with no opportunities for resitting examination papers.
Student will carry out a minimum of 16 required practicals for the combined science course or 8 for each of the separate science courses. There will no longer be any coursework or ISA assessments.
For the combined science course, there will be 6 examinations at the end of Year 11, each one being 1 hour and 15 minutes. For the separate sciences, there will be 2 exams for each science, each paper being 1 hour and 45 minutes.

The science department also try to run a range of trips for the older students trying to expand on the curriculum, for example ‘Biology in Action’. We also offer entrance into the Olympiads which are linked to the exam boards and offer a ‘stretch and challenge’ option for the students. We also direct the older students to additional lectures that are run by local universities and again offer Science material off the curriculum.

English
Curriculum Aim
"Our aim, in the English department, is to open up a rich and challenging approach to Literature and Language that will not only equip students with the knowledge and skills needed for exams, but will foster a passion for reading and writing that will be developed throughout their time at Heathside and continue into their life beyond education."
Curriculum Map
Key Stage 3 English
Students complete their assessments during one lesson, in examination conditions. They complete planning in both class and homework. In Year 9, assessments after Christmas are not planned for and are ‘unseen’ in order to prepare students for the GCSE exams.
All assessments are completed in separate writing and essay booklets. Students take these booklets home after each assessment, to be signed by parents/ guardians and then are brought back to school for safekeeping. Students are assessed on speaking and listening skills in the Summer term. A presentation on a given topic is given to the class to practise the skills needed for the GCSE award.
All students are assessed using our ‘flightpath’ system in line with DfE requirements.
Please note that, where appropriate in the units, students may watch film versions of any texts they study. This supports the range of learning needs in the classroom and helps students make other connections to the studied text. If you have any queries about this, please contact your child’s English teacher.
Key Stage 3 Progress Pathways in English
Year 7
Autumn: ‘Me, myself and I’. Students will: look at a variety of autobiography extracts; build upon writing skills such as voice, tenses and vocabulary; infer and deduce meaning from texts and use quotations; begin essay writing, learning the basic structure.
Dracula, the play. Students will: read a play based on a 19th century text; look at Gothic fiction and its context; understand the features of script writing and explore development of characters; write description to evoke atmosphere and mood.
Spring: Adventure through the Ages. Students will: look at extracts of prose from early 19th century (Jungle Book, Treasure Island) to late 21st century (Holes, Harry Potter); understand the features of Adventure fiction; identify writer’s methods and consider the effects; develop story writing to engage a reader.
Animals in poetry. Students will: read a range of poems from 19th to modern poetry about animals; identify language and structure choices made by the poets; explore ideas about meanings and interpretation; develop narrative writing to create an original and engaging ‘voice’.
Summer: The Boy in the Striped Pyjamas. Students will: focus on context and the genre of historical fiction; explore the characters in the novel and analyse how and why they have been created; begin to use comparison to develop ideas about a text; build on writing about personal experience to demonstrate engaging narrative perspective.
Introduction to Shakespeare. Students will: build on knowledge about Shakespeare and his works; Consider different points of view and opinions; Use rhetorical devices to convey an opinion to an audience.

Year 8
Autumn: Wanderlust: An Understanding of how to write in the style of travel writing is taught. Descriptive writing and comparison skills are developed. Students analyse a range of articles from different periods.
A Christmas Carol: Students read key parts of the novella. We research context; analyse the characters; identify moral messages and compare the novel to performed versions. Students develop use of imagery and tone in their writing.
Spring: Twelfth Night: Students read the text over the term, deciphering language and exploring characters. We consider themes in the play and close analysis of text. Students write as chosen characters. We explore opinions on gender stereotypes leading to persuasive writing.
Summer: The Hunger Games: Students spend time reading the novel and analysing characters, themes, context and genre. They explore the conventions of dystopian fiction and develop their awareness of its impact. Ideas about genre are applied to original writing pieces.

Autumn: Crime and Punishment: Non-fiction accounts related to Alcatraz are explored for prompts for imaginative writing. We read a Sherlock Homes short story and learn about detective fiction. Students analyse characterisation, mood and structure.
Romeo and Juliet: A focus on characters, themes and context is central to the scheme of work. Students practise their analytical understanding of Shakespeare and the key ideas of the text. Using their own experiences, students write as themselves developing tone and style.
Spring: Family in text: A range of family themed poetry is studied with a specific focus on ‘unseen’ skills in preparation for next year. Non-fiction writing on family is also explored and students learn how to convey an opinion using persuasive devices.
Journey’s End: Students study the conventions of the play, characters, plot, and setting. Understanding of the play is placed within its context. This context is then used to develop story writing skills.
Summer: Of Mice and Men. The novel is explored whilst analysing characters and plot. Particular focus is given to themes and important ideas in the text to develop critical responses. The text leads to consideration of censorship in society and students respond to this with opinion writing.

Key Stage 4 English
What is in the course?
The course has been designed to enable students of all abilities to develop the skills they need to read, understand and analyse a wide range of different texts covering the 19th, 20th and 21st century time periods as well as to write clearly, coherently and accurately using a range of vocabulary and sentence structures. The course offers excellent preparation for AS and A level English and Literature studies, as well as giving students a grounding in a wide variety of literature that will stay with them for life.
English is one of the ‘core’ subjects that all students have to study up to the end of Year 11. In fact, new Department for Education rules state that students who don’t gain a GCSE grade 4 and continue in full time education after year 11, have to continue with GCSE English and retake the course. This shows the importance which is attached to GCSE English.
All students will follow a course resulting in 2 GCSEs: English Language and English Literature.
English Language – Students will complete 3 units: Explorations in Creative Reading and Writing; Writers’ Viewpoints and Perspectives and Spoken Language.
English Literature – Students will complete 2 units: Shakespeare and the 19th- Century novel; Modern texts and poetry (including unseen poetry).
The Language and Literature GCSEs will be taught together. Students will benefit greatly from the transferable skills developed across the two subjects.
How is it assessed?
Examination Board/Course Code: AQA/Language 8700, Literature 8702
English Language – Students will be assessed through 2 examinations. Both papers are written examinations of 1 hour 45 minutes and can be awarded up to 80 marks. Each paper is worth 50% of the GCSE. The Spoken Language unit is non-examination assessment. It is marked by the teacher throughout the course and is separately endorsed. It has a 0% weighting of the GCSE.
All texts in the examination will be unseen. All examinations are un-tiered.
English Literature – Students will be assessed through 2 examinations. Paper 1 is a written examination of 1 hour 45 minutes and can be awarded up to 64 marks. It is worth 40% of the GCSE. Paper 2 is a written examination of 2 hours 15 minutes and can be awarded up to 96 marks. It is worth 60% of the GCSE.
All examinations are closed book. All examinations are un-tiered.
Extra-curricular opportunities include:
The English Department will organise theatre trips and workshops wherever possible to develop students' understanding of the texts.
Progression opportunities
Students who enjoy this subject can continue their studies at Heathside with English Literature A Level. You can find out more information on our Sixth Form Courses pages.

"Students will appreciate and understand the world in which they live and understand how to become a global citizen. Our curriculum has human and physical Geography at its core, where students explore a variety of geographical features, processes and issues at different scales. Students gain an understanding and appreciation of the cultures and background of people from all over the world. Students in Geography different opportunities for extracurricular activities. In year 7 there will be an opportunity to visit the National History Museum, where students can expand their knowledge and understanding on Tectonics, in there 8, we offer a Climate Change workshop with Jeremy Brown, who is in the process of completing his PhD about Climate Change and has written a comic book about superheros fighting climate change. Key Stage 4 Geography
What is in the course?
Geography is unique in bridging the social sciences (human geography) with the natural sciences (physical geography). In this course students will have the opportunity to develop as effective and independent learners. We aim for students to be critical and reflective thinkers with enquiring minds. Students will be able to develop their knowledge and understanding of geographical concepts and appreciate the relevance of these concepts to our changing world. In contemporary Britain it is vital that students recognise their responsibilities as global citizens and learn how they can contribute to a future that is sustainable and inclusive.
The GCSE Geography course at Heathside will help students to apply their learning to the real world through fieldwork. In order to meet the compulsory exam board requirements, we have incorporated 2 days of non-residential fieldwork and it is mandatory that all Geography students attend and participate in the fieldwork. This is completed through the Field Studies Council and the cost is approximately £50 - £80 per student.
How is it assessed?
Examination Board/Course Code: Edexcel Geography B (1GB0)
GCSE Geography Edexcel B – Investigating Geographical Issues
Three exams taken at the end of the course.
Why consider this course?
As well as being a fascinating subject, Geography equips students with a broad range of personal learning and thinking skills such as teamwork, independent enquiry and creative thinking - all highly valued by employers. Studying Geography opens up a variety of career opportunities. The analytical and research skills gained from geography are attractive to a range of employers. There are many job options for a good geographer, for example; Commercial/residential surveyor, Environmental consultant, Geographical information systems officer, Planning and development surveyor, Town planner, International aid/development worker, Logistics and distribution manager, Market researcher, Nature conservation officer, Tourism officer, Transport planner. . . and many more!
Progression opportunities
Students who enjoy this subject can continue their studies at Heathside studying A Level Geography. You can find out more information on our Sixth Form Courses pages.

One trip will be a human Geography focus and involves a visit to Guildford to investigate differences in quality of life. The other one has a physical Geography, where students visit a field study centre to then undertake fieldwork along the River Tillingbourne.

History
Curriculum Aim
History at Heathside offers an exciting curriculum taking students through the key aspects of British history, whilst also engaging with what else is going on in the world at that particular time. Enquiry questions are at the heart of every topic and cover different aspects of history from social to political. Enquiries such as: what was it like to live in a medieval town?’ to ‘why did Britain go to war in 1939?’ are analysed over a series of lessons. Whatever period of history the students are studying in Britain we also get to study what else was going on in the world at that time – for example the emancipation of the serfs in Russia in context of the abolition of slavery in Britain. The study of history ignites children’s curiosity about the past in Britain and the wider world. Through finding out about how and why the world, our country, culture and local community have developed over time, children understand how the past influences the present. History enables children to develop a context for their growing sense of identity and a chronological framework for their knowledge of significant events and people. At Heathside our intent, when teaching history, is to stimulate the children’s curiosity in order for them to develop their knowledge, skills and understanding. Running through our curriculum is also a focus on skills, so the students can improve and develop over time with a particular focus on writing analytically. Students are also encouraged to engage with history outside of the classroom too be it through visits to local historical sites, to reading history books, to watching documentaries or even being creative by building a model castle. Our curriculum is designed to leave our students informed and equipped with analytical skills and a questioning mind.

Key Stage 3 Progress Pathways in History
Year 7
Year 7 complete one written assessment each per unit. This will be completed in class and marked against flightpath descriptors. Students will record their progress across the year in the back of their books and will be tested at the end of the year in the knowledge that they have learnt. In year 7 students will be learning about the key skills of evaluating sources and analysing consequences of historical events. Students will also complete a homework menu each half term encouraging wider engagement with history,
Autumn Term 1: What is history? The Anglo-Saxons To start their year, students will look at what we mean by ‘history’ and what the key skills needed to study it are. We will then look at the use of sources by investigating the mystery of the ‘Cheddar Man’, before going on to took at the impact of the Anglo-Saxons.
Autumn Term 2: William the Conqueror
This unit will look at what Britain was like before 1066 and how William the Conqueror managed to win the Battle of Hastings against the other claimants. Students will then discover how William kept control of Britain looking at castles, the feudal system and the Domesday book.
Spring Term 1: The Middle Ages Students will explore what life was like in the Middle Ages and how the key institution of the Church influences society. Key events like the Black Death, The Magna Carta and Peasant Revolt will also be investigated.
Spring Term 2: The Crusades
This unit exemplifies the importance of the Church in the Medieval world (previous topic), by considering why people went on Crusade. This enquiry will be an evidential enquiry. This will highlight the importance of Jerusalem, threats to Byzantium and assess Pope Urban II’s call to crusade. We then focus on change and continuity, by questioning whether the Crusades changed the Holy Land. This will cover the atrocities of crusading, Muslim responses to new crusader states and individuals such as Richard I and Saladin’s impact.
Summer Term 1: The Tudors
In this unit, students will study the Tudor dynasty. They will investigate how Henry VIII changed the face of religion in England by breaking from Rome. They will identify the reasons behind the changes in religion under the Tudors and consider their consequences. They will also consider the success of Elizabeth I’s reign.
This unit will be the main focus on the ‘End of Year Exam’. Students will need an in-depth knowledge of this topic.
Summer Term 2: World Study: The Aztecs
As part of a world study, Students will learn about the Aztecs – The rise and fall of the civilisation and how they society functioned.

In this unit Students will study reasons for the growing tension between the King and parliament which resulted in a bitter civil war and the execution of a King. Students will then assess the brief reign of Oliver Cromwell and why eventually the monarchy returned in the Glorious Revolution in 1688.
Autumn Term 2: Empire and Slavery
This unit will look at the expansion of Britain and the creation of the British Empire. The different explorers, their voyages, destinations and impact on the indigenous population will all be assessed. Students will also complete a depth study on the horrors of slavery and reasons for its final abolition in Britain.
Spring Term 1: Democracy In Britain 1800 - 1928
Students will investigate how democracy changes during the period 1800 – 1928, looking at the impact of the Great Reform Act 1834, The Chartists and votes for women.
Spring Term 2: The Industrial Revolution
Students will explore what life was like in Industrial Britain looking at the positive and negative aspects it brings to people’s lives. The changes in transportation, from agriculture to industry, the many wonderful inventions and the problems urbanisation and industrialisation bring to Britain will all be assessed.
Summer Term 1&2: World Study, Civil Rights in USA
Students will complete a world study on the civil rights movement sweeping America in the 20th century, looking at changes in education, civil and political rights and the key individuals/protest movements involved in pushing change.
This unit will be the main focus on the ‘End of Year Exam’. Students will need an in-depth knowledge of this topic.

Key Stage 3 Design & Technology
Key Stage 3 Progress Pathways in Design & Technology
Throughout Year 7 and 8, our students study 5 areas of Design and Technology: Engineering, Food Preparation and Nutrition, Graphics, Product Design and Textiles. Projects are on a rotational basis lasting approximately 7-8 weeks.
At the end of year 8 students will opt to complete two of the five subjects to study in more detail over one term per subject throughout year 9. Students will have the opportunity to select one of the five Design and Technology subjects as a GCSE option.
All subjects in years 7, 8 and 9 are assessed in the following areas: Design, Make, Evaluate and Technical knowledge. They will then have an overall level based on those 4 assessment strands.
Year 7
Engineering: Students are introduced to Engineering and they explore mechanisms, gain experience in card modelling and computer aided design in order to design and make a cam toy.
Food Preparation and Nutrition: Students are introduced to the kitchen and related Health and Safety rules. Students will perform a series of practical tasks to broaden their skills base and cook a repertoire of predominantly savoury dishes so that they are able to feed themselves and others a healthy and varied diet.
Graphics: Students are introduced to a range of technical drawing skills and card modelling techniques used in Graphics. Students then will design and create their own Cubeecraft character model and have an opportunity to use computer aided design to create advertising for their designs.
Product Design: Students are introduced to materials and their properties, brazing and lathe work, culminating in the production of an individually designed toy that must balance on a pedestal.
Textiles: Students will be learning how to make fabrics from scratch. The felt that they make will then be used to applique the features of their phone case cover. They will be enhancing their hand embroidery skills.
Year 8
Engineering: Building upon previous skills, students create a programmable steady hand game that counts the number of lives lost and plays a tune when complete. The focus of this project is independence when making to be able to solder and programme confidently.
Food Preparation and Nutrition: The students continue to learn many new skills when making a variety of food and Health and Safety when cooking and are introduced to the science of food and food investigation. This helps them to understand the function of ingredients and will cook a repertoire of predominantly savoury dishes.
Graphics: Students learn about the importance of logo branding and packaging design in this project so that they can design and make a product packaging of their own. They will learn to use 2D Design and Adobe Photoshop computer aided design software to create their graphic designs. Card modelling and craft knife skills are used to complete their final product.
Product Design: Through the use of computer aided design and manufacture, workshop tools and machines, students will design and make their very own professional high quality decorative box. This project introduces students to pewter casting and the use of computer aided design and manufacture with the laser cutter to incorporate marquetry.
Textiles: Students will be using inspiration from African culture, learning about traditional block printing and tie dying to produce their very own cultural cushion cover. In addition to these techniques, the students will also learn safe use of the sewing machine and revisit decorative processes to personalise their designs.
Year 9
Engineering: This unit expands skills already learnt and students design and make their own steady hand game using commercial PCB design software and computer aided design. They will create their circuit and solder the components on to get the circuit working. They will be able to program the game to have several sound and light outputs. There is an emphasis on engineering principals, such as calculations and problem solving.
Food Preparation and Nutrition: This unit will teach the students the importance of developing practical skills, healthy eating and nutrition. They will be taught a variety of practical skills and will learn how to be able to produce several healthy meals. Students will be introduced to a range of useful skills that they will need to produce main meals and desserts. Some of the skills that are covered include making your own sauces from scratch, knife skills, how to cook different types of meals using meat, or meat alternatives and much more. Extended project looking at Global Cuisines, embedding the multicultural nature of Food in UK. Culminating in a research and design written project and dedicated practical.
Graphics: Students will expand upon their graphical communication skills learnt previously to design and produce an advertising campaign for an event of their choice. The students will learn about brand identity, graphic design and designers, the art of typography and poster design. They develop their drawing and presentation skills to help communicate ideas and developing their skills in layout design and paper and card modelling. There is a strong emphasis on computer aided design to produce their graphic design work; learning to use Adobe Illustrator to create digital drawing and icons and can revisit their skills in Adobe Photoshop to edit photos or paint realistic artwork to produce their final pieces.
Product Design: In Year 9 this unit focuses on both design creativity and manufacture to create their very own desk lamp or task light using low voltage LED lighting unit. Students will learn how to work with woods and metals and in particular, the use of upcycled materials to create their design ideas with a range of machines and hand tools. Students learn about the material families, sustainability, designing with drawing and computer aided design and revisit their PCB soldering skills to produce their outcome.
Textiles: In Textiles students will expand upon previous sewing machine skills and learn a variety of decorative techniques; including couching, weaving, chenilling, foiling, reverse applique amongst many others. In this unit students design and make a festival bucket hat using recycled materials; focussing on the impact that the Textiles industry has on the environment. There may also be the opportunity to explore computerised textiles techniques such as the computer aided manufacture embroidery machine, the laser cutter and digital transfer printing. Students will create a product from scratch, devising their own paper templates to develop their special awareness and ability to create a 3D structure from a 2D design.

Throughout the year a weekly DT club is offered to KS3 inviting students to extend their learning outside of the classroom in Design and Technology. As like the subject, DT club offers the topic areas within Design and Technology on a rotational basis where students can learn and create fun outcomes. Projects include Food Science, Tunnocks Teacake national competition, Graphics club learning digital illustration using the Adobe suite and Textiles club learning embroidery skills to make textiles products.

What is in the course?
The Food Preparation and Nutrition GCSE is an exciting and creative course which focuses on practical cooking skills and will ensure students develop greater understanding of nutrition, food provenance and the working characteristics of food materials. Students will also learn about British and international culinary traditions, food security and food safety. At the heart of the qualification is a focus on developing practical cookery skills and a strong understanding of nutrition. The specification has been organised into the following sections:
• Food Preparation Skills • Food, Nutrition and Health • Food Safety • Food Science • Food Provenance • Food Choice
Students will be expected to take part in practicals every week in year 10, and as part of their nonexam assessments in year 11. Students will be required to bring all their own ingredients and where applicable equipment to transport home. Students are expected to have a suitable apron.
How is it assessed?
Exam Board - AQA Specification Code – 8585 QAN Code – 601/8421/8
How it’s assessed 50% Exam and 50% Non-Exam Assessment
Single examination paper - 1hr 45 minutes duration Section A (20 marks) Multiple Choice Questions – structured to reflect the sections of the specification. Section B (80 marks) – 5 questions varying in styles of approach and content.
Non-Exam Assessment - Two tasks The Food Investigation (15%) Recommended time 10 hours The Food Preparation Assessment (35%) Recommended time 20 hours (including 3-hour practical period)
The Non-Exam Assessments are taken in Year 11 only
Why consider this course?
The food industry is a large employer, offering many different opportunities. It will enable you to use and develop skills you will have gained over the two years of study, into everyday life or into a worthwhile career. There are further education courses locally – Brooklands – City and Guilds qualifications and South Thames College, Merton who offer a variety of NVQ’s. Opportunities at University level e.g. BSc (Hons) Culinary Science at University of Birmingham, BA (Hons) Food Business Entrepreneurship at Manchester Metropolitan University, BSc (Hons) in Food Science and Technology at Nottingham Trent University and BSc (Hons) Nutrition and Food Science at the University of Surrey and Apprenticeships e.g. MARS Manufacturing Apprenticeships or Nestle Food Manufacturing Apprentice.

The fine motor skills of practical skill development have been positively accepted by further education establishment for students who want to go into Medicine/Veterinary Science and Engineering as a career path.

Graphic Communication
What is in the course?
Graphic Communication introduces students to a visual way of conveying information, ideas and emotions, using a range of graphic media, processes, techniques and elements such as colour, icons, images, typography and photographs. Students explore traditional and new technologies, where all work will be documented in their sketchbooks, meeting the four assessment objectives.

Externally set assignment (40%): This is made up of two parts: preparation and final piece. Students will need to prepare a sketchbook based on an unseen topic that they have selected to show their ideas and development. Students will use their experimentations and ideas for their final piece which must be completed within 10 hours under exam conditions. The exam will be over two days.

Religious Studies
Curriculum Aim Religious Studies in Key Stage 3
Fostering Understanding and Respect: Religious Education (RE) in Key Stage 3 plays a pivotal role in fostering an environment of understanding and respect among students. It provides them with a comprehensive understanding of different religions, beliefs, and worldviews.
By exploring a diverse range of religious traditions and practices, students develop an appreciation for cultural and religious diversity, which is essential in our increasingly globalized and multicultural society. This understanding is crucial for promoting social cohesion and preparing students to become respectful and empathetic global citizens.
Critical Thinking and Ethical Reflection: Another core purpose of RE in Key Stage 3 is to cultivate critical thinking and ethical reflection. Through engaging with various religious and philosophical questions, students are encouraged to think deeply about moral and ethical issues, enhancing their ability to reason and articulate their own beliefs and values.
This intellectual engagement helps students develop important skills such as critical analysis, debate, and reflection. It empowers them to make informed and thoughtful decisions in their personal and public lives, contributing positively to society.
Personal Development and Spiritual Growth: RE also plays a significant role in the personal development and spiritual growth of students. It offers a safe space for students to explore their own beliefs and values in the context of learning about others. This self-reflective process helps students gain a deeper understanding of themselves and their place in the world.
By encountering and reflecting on different religious perspectives, students are encouraged to think about their own spiritual and moral development, which is integral to their overall well-being and personal growth.
Promoting Community and Active Citizenship: Furthermore, RE in Key Stage 3 promotes a sense of community and active citizenship. It encourages students to engage with and contribute to their communities with a sense of responsibility and care. By understanding the principles and practices of various faiths, students learn the importance of tolerance, compassion, and mutual respect.
These values are crucial for building harmonious communities and fostering an inclusive society. Moreover, RE equips students with the knowledge and skills to challenge prejudice and discrimination, thereby promoting equality and justice.
Holistic Education and Preparation for Future Learning: Finally, RE contributes to a holistic education, preparing students for further learning and life beyond school. It complements other areas of the curriculum by enhancing students’ cultural literacy and social awareness. The skills and knowledge gained in RE are transferable and valuable across various academic disciplines and in everyday life. By engaging with the rich tapestry of human belief and experience, students are better prepared for future academic pursuits and for navigating the complexities of the modern world.
Religious Education in Key Stage 3 aligns with our goal on providing a broad, balanced, and ambitious curriculum that nurtures well-rounded, informed, and thoughtful individuals. This takes influence from the latest guidance provided by the Surrey SACRE and will be continued to be updated to absorb and reflect the most up to date guidance. This looks at ways of exploring topics using a range of Sociological, Philosophical and Theological lenses.
Parents and carers can withdraw their children from any/all RE lessons.

Why consider this course?

Throughout their time in Computer Science students develop the problem solving skills that universities and employers are looking for. Computer Science dovetails well with a variety of other subjects, especially the Sciences, Mathematics and Art & Design. The Music Department offers a busy programme of extra-curricular activities throughout the week. Key Stage 4 Music
What is in the course?
The GCSE Music course is divided into three components – performing, composing and listening – with one lesson per week being assigned to each discipline. Over the two-year course, students will study general musical history and theory as well as developing in-depth knowledge and understanding of eight musical works from four different Areas of Study through performing, composing and listening activities.
Area of Study: Instrumental Music 1700-1820 1. J.S. Bach: 3rd movement from Brandenburg Concerto no.5 in D major 2. Beethoven: 1st movement of Piano Sonata no.8 in C minor ‘Pathétique’
Area of Study: Vocal Music 3. Purcell: Music for a While 4. Queen: Killer Queen
Area of Study: Music for Stage and Screen 5. Schwartz: Defying Gravity 6. Williams: Main title/ rebel blockade runner (from Star Wars)
Area of Study: Fusions 7. Afro Celt Sound System: Release 8. Esperanza Spalding: Samba Em Preludio
Students opting to take GCSE Music must be working at Grade 3 level on at least one instrument and must be having regular lessons, either in school or with an external teacher. Students are also expected to take part in the many performing opportunities offered at Heathside.
How is it assessed?
Examination Board/Course Code: Edexcel/1MU0
Performing makes up 30% of the GCSE course and consists of two submissions at the end of Year 11. Students are assessed continually throughout the two years in both solo and ensemble performance.
Composing makes up 30% of the GCSE course with students composing three compositions over the two years, of which they submit two for external assessment. One of the compositions is to a set brief by the exam board, the other is a free composition.
Listening makes up 40% of the GCSE course. It is examined in a 1hour 45-minute written examination which is set and marked by the Exam Board and is based on the eight set works that the students have been studying. In Section A (68 marks) of the paper, students will respond to questions based on the recorded extracts of some of the set works. They will also complete a melodic and rhythmic dictation question and answer a listening-based question on an unfamiliar piece of music. In Section B (12 marks), students answer a more in-depth question (essay-based) comparing and evaluating the musical elements, musical contexts and musical language of one set work with one unfamiliar piece of music.
Why consider this course?
The Music option at GCSE is a development of the work studied at Key Stage 3 and a stepping stone for further study at AS and A Level and potentially a career in a musical field. The course aims to develop students’ understanding and appreciation of a wide range of musical genres and styles and encourages critical and creative thinking.
Progression Opportunities:
